item.title: Isahaya Onsen Hot Springs — Guide
item.description: Isahaya, a town on the neck of land between Nagasaki city, Shimabara and the Ariake Sea, offers a quieter, more local hot-spring experience away from the bigger resorts. Its baths and inns let visitors soak in relaxing waters at an unhurried pace, making it a pleasant overnight or rest stop for travellers crossing the region — for instance on the way to the Shimabara Peninsula and Unzen. Isahaya is also known for its lovely Isahaya Park and the historic Meganebashi, a graceful double-arched stone ‘spectacles bridge’ reflected in the water, one of Japan’s oldest of its kind.

item.title: Kumamoto Tea Country — Guide
item.description: The highlands of the Aso region and Kumamoto’s mountains are dotted with beautiful green-tea plantations, where neat rows of tea bushes carpet the rolling hills in vivid green. Kumamoto produces well-regarded Japanese green tea, and its cool, misty upland climate and volcanic soils are ideal for cultivating it. In tea-growing villages, visitors can take in the scenic terraced fields, especially lovely in the fresh green of the new-leaf season in late spring, learn about tea cultivation and processing, and — depending on the spot — sample or buy fresh local tea, enjoy tea-flavoured sweets, or join seasonal tea-picking experiences.

item.title: Takayama Onsen: A Quiet Country Hot Spring — Guide
item.description: Takayama Onsen is a quiet country hot spring in the Mine area of central Yamaguchi, the same rural district as the Akiyoshido cave and Akiyoshidai plateau. Away from the big resort towns, hot springs like this offer something increasingly rare: an unhurried, unpretentious soak surrounded by hills and fields, favoured by locals rather than tour groups. A warm bath in mineral waters, the quiet of the countryside, and perhaps a simple meal or an overnight in a modest inn make it a restful counterpoint to a day exploring the karst landscape nearby.

item.title: Furano & Biei Guide: Flower Fields, Hills & Best Time
item.description: In central Hokkaido, Furano and Biei are the postcard image of the island’s countryside — a gently rolling patchwork of fields that ripple to the horizon beneath big skies and distant mountains. Furano is famous for its summer flower fields, above all the purple sweep of lavender, while neighbouring Biei enchants with sculpted hills, lone trees and the surreal Blue Pond. Whether you drive the panorama roads, cycle the lanes or ride the seasonal train, this is one of Japan’s most beautiful rural landscapes.

item.title: Tottori Hidden Gems: Secret Beaches, White Walls & Mountain Villages
item.description: Tottori’s fame stops at the sand dunes for most visitors. That’s understandable — they’re extraordinary. But the prefecture’s most lasting impressions often come from somewhere else: a riverside district of white-plastered sake warehouses untouched since the Edo period, a temple wedged impossibly into a cliff cave, a razor-thin strip of sand that separates a lake from the open sea. These places require a little planning and occasionally some nerve, but they offer what crowded attractions cannot — the feeling that you’ve actually found something.
